blocks.text: Keep three questions separate throughout this volume. What does an object mean? Who keeps its resources alive? Which operations are expensive enough to matter? A design can answer the first two correctly before measuring the third. Reversing that order often produces clever code whose result is unclear. This chapter establishes the vocabulary used in the remaining chapters, especially the distinction between a copied value, a borrowed object, and a transferred resource.

reading.title: Chapter overview
paragraphs: The first task ledger worked without a single raw owning pointer. That is not a temporary beginner shortcut. It demonstrates a central modern C++ idea: use types that already express ownership and useful behavior, then inspect costs where requirements make them relevant.

topics.title: 1.1 Understanding Zero-Cost Abstractions
topics.summary: An abstraction provides a useful model while hiding irrelevant implementation details. A vector exposes an owned sequence instead of making every caller manage allocation and element destruction. A generic algorithm exposes an operation over a range instead of repeating traversal mechanics at every call site.

blocks.text: Suppose a report sums the priorities of the open tasks. A counted loop exposes an index, a boundary, an accumulator, and the update operation. An algorithm call exposes the same traversal through a smaller interface. Neither spelling determines how many memory allocations the surrounding program performs. If one version first copies a million records and the other borrows them, a timing comparison primarily measures that semantic difference, not the cost of the loop abstraction.

blocks.text: Define a fair comparison before reaching for a stopwatch. Both implementations should receive the same elements, use the same accumulation type, apply the same overflow policy, and return the same result. They should either both include dataset preparation or both exclude it. If the required answer fits in long long but the handwritten version accumulates in int, equal results on a tiny fixture do not establish equivalence over the intended domain.

blocks.text: There are several kinds of cost. A checked accessor may perform a conditional test. A container can allocate capacity. A type-erased callable can require indirect dispatch. A debug iterator can carry bookkeeping absent from a release configuration. These are different mechanisms and cannot be evaluated with the sentence “C++ is fast.” Identify the mechanism and the environment, then inspect or measure it. The worked example deliberately checks results rather than reporting an unearned speedup.

topics.title: 1.1.2 Understanding Compile-Time Optimization
topics.summary: constexpr allows suitable functions and objects to participate in constant evaluation. A static_assert can require a particular expression to be evaluated as a constant expression and reject an invalid property during translation. A constexpr function can also execute at runtime when given runtime inputs.

cards.question: Explain Understanding Compile-Time Optimization in your own words.
cards.answer: constexpr allows suitable functions and objects to participate in constant evaluation. A static_assert can require a particular expression to be evaluated as a constant expression and reject an invalid property during translation. A constexpr function can also execute at runtime when given runtime inputs.

blocks.text: constexpr allows suitable functions and objects to participate in constant evaluation. blocks.text: Do not confuse this language facility with the optimizer’s freedom to fold ordinary expressions. A compiler can optimize computations that are not declared constexpr, while a constexpr declaration does not force every call to disappear from runtime. The example uses static_assert(square(7) == 49) to state an actual compile-time requirement over a small representable input.

blocks.text: A compile-time requirement is useful when violating it should prevent the executable from existing. Consider a fixed packet layout whose field counts must add up to an expected total. An assertion over constants can reject a mistaken layout during the build. That is different from a runtime validation of a length read from a file. The former concerns the program’s construction; the latter concerns information not known until execution.

An assertion over constants can reject a mistaken layout during the build. That is different from a runtime validation of a length read from a file. The former concerns the program’s construction; the latter concerns information not known until execution.

blocks.text: The declaration constexpr int square(int x) does not promise that every integer input can be squared safely. If signed multiplication overflows, the expression is not made valid by the keyword. A constant-expression context can reject some invalid computations, while a runtime call still needs the program’s usual domain rules. Our example chooses seven specifically because its square is representable. Later chapters add checked arithmetic rather than silently extending this small demonstration into a universal numeric utility.

Larger template instantiations and constant computations can reduce repeated runtime work while increasing compiler memory use, build time, or binary size. For HarborWorks, a table that rarely changes may be a good candidate for precomputation. A table supplied by a customer is not suddenly a compile-time object because precomputation sounds efficient. topics.chapterTitle: Understanding the Philosophy of Modern C++
topics.title: 1.2 Designing Around Value Semantics
topics.summary: Value semantics make an object behave as an independently meaningful value. Copying a point should ordinarily give another point whose later coordinates can change independently. This makes local reasoning and rollback easier because one value is not silently tied to another’s mutable identity.

blocks.text: This behavior follows the member types’ semantics. A struct containing a raw pointer copies the pointer value, not the pointed-to object. Therefore a class does not acquire deep value semantics merely because its syntax looks like a record. Inspect each member’s ownership role before deciding what copying the enclosing object means.

blocks.text: Treat a report snapshot as a small contract. After making snapshot B from dataset A, a change to B’s title must not alter A’s title. Destroying A must not make B unusable. Saving B should not accidentally read a later revision of A. Those requirements make an owning value representation attractive: a vector of records whose titles are strings provides independent nested values without custom allocation code.

blocks.text: Independence does not require different values at the moment of copying. Immediately after the copy, A and B can compare equal. The distinction is what happens after mutation or destruction. A good copy test therefore has at least two phases: establish equality, then change one side and verify that the other preserves its previous value. Merely comparing their sizes immediately after construction is too weak to detect shared storage.

blocks.text: Value semantics also have limits. A copied record may contain an identifier for an external database row. Copying the identifier does not copy the external database. A copied filesystem path does not duplicate the file it names. Be explicit about the boundary of the value: the C++ object can be independent even while both values refer to the same external identity. This is why resource ownership and application identity need separate diagrams rather than one ambiguous arrow labelled “has.”

topics.title: 1.2.2 Distinguishing Value and Reference Semantics
topics.summary: Reference semantics emphasize access to an existing object’s identity. A reference to the first point observes that point rather than creating another point. Its validity depends on the owner’s lifetime and relevant invalidation rules.

cards.question: Explain Distinguishing Value and Reference Semantics in your own words.
cards.answer: Reference semantics emphasize access to an existing object’s identity. A reference to the first point observes that point rather than creating another point. Its validity depends on the owner’s lifetime and relevant invalidation rules.

blocks.text: 1.2.2 Distinguishing Value and Reference Semantics

blocks.text: Neither model is universally superior. Use values when independence is intended, and references when borrowing an existing object is intended. Mixing the two without naming the relationship causes defects: a supposed snapshot unexpectedly reflects later changes, or an observer dangles after its source reallocates. Interfaces should make that choice visible.

Mixing the two without naming the relationship causes defects: a supposed snapshot unexpectedly reflects later changes, or an observer dangles after its source reallocates. Interfaces should make that choice visible.

blocks.text: A borrow is often the correct choice for a function that only formats an existing report during the call. Passing a large report by const reference can avoid creating another owned dataset. The formatter does not decide when the report is destroyed and must not save an internal address for later use unless the interface establishes a longer lifetime contract.

The formatter does not decide when the report is destroyed and must not save an internal address for later use unless the interface establishes a longer lifetime contract.

blocks.text: The type alone does not express every part of that contract. A const reference prevents certain modifications through that access path, but another alias may still change the underlying object. It also does not stop the owner from being destroyed after the function returns. A retained callback that refers to a local report can therefore be wrong even though every reference is const and the program compiled cleanly.

blocks.text: Use an ownership timeline when a diagram becomes ambiguous. Mark the report’s creation, the start and finish of a borrowing call, any container mutation, and destruction. Every use of a borrowed element must occur while the element is alive and the particular reference remains valid. In a vector, the owner’s lifetime is necessary but not sufficient: reallocation can invalidate references while the vector itself continues to exist. Chapters 14–18 return to this distinction for closures, iterators, and views.

paragraphs: Reference semantics emphasize access to an existing object’s identity. A reference to the first point observes that point rather than creating another point. Its validity depends on the owner’s lifetime and relevant invalidation rules.

Neither model is universally superior. Use values when independence is intended, and references when borrowing an existing object is intended. Mixing the two without naming the relationship causes defects: a supposed snapshot unexpectedly reflects later changes, or an observer dangles after its source reallocates. Interfaces should make that choice visible.

A borrow is often the correct choice for a function that only formats an existing report during the call. Passing a large report by const reference can avoid creating another owned dataset. The formatter does not decide when the report is destroyed and must not save an internal address for later use unless the interface establishes a longer lifetime contract.

The type alone does not express every part of that contract. A const reference prevents certain modifications through that access path, but another alias may still change the underlying object. It also does not stop the owner from being destroyed after the function returns. A retained callback that refers to a local report can therefore be wrong even though every reference is const and the program compiled cleanly.

Use an ownership timeline when a diagram becomes ambiguous. Mark the report’s creation, the start and finish of a borrowing call, any container mutation, and destruction. Every use of a borrowed element must occur while the element is alive and the particular reference remains valid. In a vector, the owner’s lifetime is necessary but not sufficient: reallocation can invalidate references while the vector itself continues to exist. Chapters 14–18 return to this distinction for closures, iterators, and views.

topics.title: 1.3 Managing Ownership Explicitly

blocks.text: List resources rather than just pointers. The input stream has an open-file resource, the candidate dataset owns strings and vector storage, the output stream has an external destination, and an error object may own diagnostic text. A raw pointer used to choose between std::cin and a locally owned file can be a legitimate non-owning selector; it is not automatically a defect merely because a raw pointer appears.

blocks.text: For each resource, identify the release operation and the owner that invokes it. A vector destroys its elements and releases its storage. A stream object closes its associated file as part of its cleanup. An exclusive native-handle wrapper invokes the matching native release function. If the design cannot name the owner, it has not finished designing the failure paths.

blocks.text: Then ask whether ownership changes. Passing an object for inspection need not transfer anything. Returning a newly constructed value hands a result to the caller. Moving a unique pointer transfers one explicit responsibility. Copying a shared pointer adds a participant in shared lifetime management, not an independently allocated copy of the pointee. These distinctions make function signatures reviewable before reading the entire implementation.

topics.title: 1.3.2 Avoiding Ambiguous Ownership
topics.summary: Ambiguous ownership appears when a function accepts a raw pointer and callers cannot tell whether it will delete, retain, or merely inspect the object. Improve the interface or document a narrow borrowing contract rather than relying on naming alone.

cards.question: Explain Avoiding Ambiguous Ownership in your own words.
cards.answer: Ambiguous ownership appears when a function accepts a raw pointer and callers cannot tell whether it will delete, retain, or merely inspect the object. Improve the interface or document a narrow borrowing contract rather than relying on naming alone.

blocks.text: 1.3.2 Avoiding Ambiguous Ownership
rich: 1.3.2 Avoiding Ambiguous Ownership

blocks.text: Ambiguous ownership appears when a function accepts a raw pointer and callers cannot tell whether it will delete, retain, or merely inspect the object. Improve the interface or document a narrow borrowing contract rather than relying on naming alone.
rich: Ambiguous ownership appears when a function accepts a raw pointer and callers cannot tell whether it will delete, retain, or merely inspect the object. Improve the interface or document a narrow borrowing contract rather than relying on naming alone.

blocks.text: A parameter accepting an ordinary reference usually communicates borrowing for the call. A value parameter can own its local value. A smart-pointer parameter should be used when the ownership relationship itself is relevant to the operation, not simply because the caller happens to store the object in a smart pointer. Borrow the object directly when lifetime participation is unnecessary.
rich: A parameter accepting an ordinary reference usually communicates borrowing for the call. A value parameter can own its local value. A smart-pointer parameter should be used when the ownership relationship itself is relevant to the operation, not simply because the caller happens to store the object in a smart pointer. Borrow the object directly when lifetime participation is unnecessary.

blocks.text: Ambiguity often enters through “convenient” helper functions. Imagine install_report(Report* p). Does the function inspect the report, store the pointer, delete the report on failure, or assume ownership only on success? Each policy can be implemented, but callers cannot safely guess which one was selected. A parameter representing an owned value or a unique owner can make a transfer visible. A reference plus an explicit no-retention contract can make synchronous borrowing visible.
rich: Ambiguity often enters through “convenient” helper functions. Imagine

Each policy can be implemented, but callers cannot safely guess which one was selected. A parameter representing an owned value or a unique owner can make a transfer visible. A reference plus an explicit no-retention contract can make synchronous borrowing visible.

blocks.text: Avoid solving that ambiguity by putting shared pointers into every signature. A formatting function that only needs a report’s values should not force stack-allocated callers to invent shared ownership. Conversely, a background task that must keep a report alive after the caller returns needs a real lifetime arrangement; accepting a reference and hoping the caller waits is not a substitute.

A formatting function that only needs a report’s values should not force stack-allocated callers to invent shared ownership. Conversely, a background task that must keep a report alive after the caller returns needs a real lifetime arrangement; accepting a reference and hoping the caller waits is not a substitute.

blocks.text: Review ownership on failure as carefully as on success. If a consuming operation takes a value parameter, the caller may already have moved its source before the function begins validation. Rejecting the operation does not automatically restore the caller’s old object. A design that promises preservation should validate before transferring, or stage a separate candidate. The transaction examples later in the book make this boundary explicit.

reading.title: Failure clinic — A snapshot that was not a snapshot
paragraphs: An engineer changes Point so its x coordinate is represented by a pointer to an external integer. The compiler still generates copy operations, and the vector still owns its point objects. Yet the independence test now fails because both points designate the same external integer. The vector did not malfunction. The meaning of copying one element changed.

Repair the model at the level of the requirement. If a coordinate is a value, store the integer as a value. If the point intentionally observes a shared measurement, rename and document the observation relationship rather than pretending it is a snapshot. Replacing the pointer with shared_ptr<int> keeps the integer alive but still does not create independent integer values when the point is copied.

topics.summary: The strongest evidence for independence is a change to one value that does not affect the other, followed by use of the survivor after the source is gone. Const qualification does not supply lifetime. Shared ownership does not supply deep copying. An optimization observation does not redefine a language contract. Keep those three distinctions in the written acceptance notes; they recur throughout the book.

overview.explanation: Dashed arrows show compile-time dependencies on a type or function. There is no inheritance and no heap ownership in this example.

focus.title: State what equality means
focus.code:
struct UserId{ int value; };
bool operator==(UserId a, UserId b){ return a.value==b.value; }
explain: struct creates the UserId type. Its value member is public by default. The semicolon ends the type declaration.
operator== defines equality for two UserId values. The parameters are copies; comparing their integer fields produces a bool result.
focus.what: The wrapper gives a name and type to the meaning “user identifier.”
focus.where: The declarations appear before the call in main, so the compiler can resolve a==b.
focus.why: The type makes intent visible. For a small identifier, copying is simpler than managing pointers.
focus.invariant: Two identifiers with the same value compare equal. Equality must be consistent wherever the type is used.
focus.risk: Comparing addresses would compare objects’ locations rather than identifier values. A public field allows arbitrary integers, so this type alone does not enforce valid user ranges.

focus.title: Call the type’s equality operation
focus.code: int main(){ UserId a{7}, b{7}; std::cout << std::boolalpha << (a==b) << '\n'; }
explain: Braces initialize two separate UserId objects with the value 7. a==b calls the overload. std::boolalpha makes the stream print true instead of 1, followed by a newline.
focus.what: The caller observes equality without depending on the comparison’s spelling.
focus.where: This is the entry point and the complete output-producing call.
focus.why: A named type helps separate user identifiers from unrelated integers in larger interfaces.
focus.invariant: Both objects live until main returns; no reference escapes. The expected output is true.
focus.risk: Changing operator== to compare another property changes every caller’s meaning of equality.
